Oersted’s Discovery
Magnetic Field Around a Straight Wire
Magnetic Field Patterns

items.text: In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted made a surprising observation during a classroom demonstration. When he passed electric current through a wire, a nearby compass needle moved, showing that the electric current created a magnetic effect. This discovery revealed that electricity and magnetism are linked, leading to the development of electromagnetism—a foundation of modern technology.
items.title: Oersted’s Discovery
items.alt: Oersted’s Discovery. A compass near a current-carrying wire responds to the wire’s magnetic field.

items.text: When electric current flows through a straight wire, it creates a magnetic field that circles around the wire. You can use the right-hand rule: point your thumb in the direction of the current, and your fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field lines. This helps predict how the field will behave around the wire.
items.title: Magnetic Field Around a Straight Wire
items.alt: Magnetic Field Around a Straight Wire. Right-hand rule: thumb follows conventional current; curled fingers show B.

items.text: The magnetic field around a straight wire forms circular loops centered on the wire. The direction of these loops depends on the direction of the current. If you reverse the current, the magnetic field direction also reverses. This pattern is key to understanding how electromagnets work and how we can control magnetic fields with electricity.
items.title: Magnetic Field Patterns
items.alt: Magnetic Field Patterns. Reversing the current reverses the circular magnetic-field direction.

items.text: For the same coil and core, increasing current generally strengthens the magnetic field. In the practice investigation, current is changed from 0.50 A to 1.00 A while the coil and pickup method remain fixed. Test the prediction using clip counts.
items.title: Current
items.alt: Current. With the same coil and core, greater current generally strengthens the magnetic field.

items.text: At the same current and similar coil geometry, more turns can produce a stronger field. In a battery-powered design, extra turns also add wire length, resistance, and cost. Current can fall. Measure the result and compare clips per cost instead of assuming that the most turns must win.
items.title: Coil Turns
items.alt: Coil Turns. More turns can strengthen the field at fixed current; a fixed battery adds a resistance tradeoff.

items.text: An iron core becomes magnetized and strengthens the field compared with an air core in the same coil. Compare the assigned Trials 1 and 3. If voltage and wire resistance stay the same, changing the core need not change current. Use both clip counts to support your explanation.
items.title: Core Material
items.alt: Core Material. An iron core can strengthen the field without changing the circuit current.

items.text: The field generally weakens farther from the electromagnet. In a physical clip-lifting test, keep contact position, lift height, and timing consistent. Otherwise a changed pickup method can affect the count even when the electrical settings are unchanged.
items.title: Distance
items.alt: Distance. Keep pickup distance and method fixed when comparing lifting performance.

items.text:
Choose before opening: compare Trials 1 and 3, or Trials 1 and 4?

Use Trials 1 and 3. Core material changes while turns, core diameter, cells, and wiring stay fixed. Compare both current and clip counts. Trials 1 and 4 change the power source.
items.title: Which comparison isolates the core effect?
items.alt: Trials 1 and 3 use the same coil and electrical setup; only the core changes from iron to air. Compare both current and lifting results.

items.text:
Predict: with the same battery, does doubling turns also keep current unchanged?

No. Extra wire increases resistance, so current can fall. Record current as an outcome of the design change. “More turns at the same current” and “more turns on the same battery” are different comparisons.
items.title: Does adding turns keep current constant?
items.alt: A coil with more turns uses more wire. With the same battery, added resistance can reduce current.

items.text:
Your best checked design uses an iron core. To investigate the effect of core diameter, should you also change its cells and turns?

Keep cells, wiring, turns, and core material fixed. Change core diameter, predict the effect, run the test, and check value. Keep the better design as your reference, then investigate another setting. Three designs are a minimum, not a guarantee of reaching 6.38.
items.title: What should you test next?
items.alt: Predict an outcome, change one setting, test and check the calculations, then retain or refine the best design.

items.text:
A design lifts more clips after both the core and cell arrangement change. Can you conclude that the core alone caused the increase?

No. You found a better combination, but both changes could contribute. Run a matched comparison changing only core material to support a causal explanation.
items.title: Can one improved design prove a cause?
items.alt: Changing both an air core to iron and one cell to two can improve a design but cannot isolate the effect of either change.

The assigned simulation reports clips lifted as a classroom measure of lifting performance. It is not a direct magnetic-field measurement in tesla or a guarantee of real hardware performance. Record the displayed count exactly before interpreting it.

+

items.text: Record the displayed clips lifted exactly. This is a classroom measure of lifting performance, not a direct magnetic-field measurement in tesla or a guarantee of real hardware performance.
items.title: Measuring Lifting Performance
items.alt: Measuring Magnetic Strength. Clips lifted measure lifting performance; they are not a direct measurement of B in tesla.

items.text: In a physical experiment, repeats reveal variation and support a mean. In this deterministic simulation, identical settings may return the same result. Trial 6 requires at least three different designs, not three repeats of one design.
items.title: Repeating Trials
items.alt: Repeating Trials. Physical repeats reveal variation. Identical inputs in a deterministic model may repeat exactly.

items.text: For the fictional physical test, changes in clip contact or lift height could affect results. A guide and consistent timing address those limits. For the simulation, discuss the limits of the model and of the settings you tested; do not invent measurement variation or equipment failures.
items.title: Controlling Uncertainty
items.alt: Controlling Uncertainty. Control physical measurement conditions; evaluate simulation limits without inventing random failures.

items.text: Prepare one record per trial or design: turns; core material; core diameter (mm); cell count and arrangement; current; clips lifted; displayed cost; wire length; and clips per cost. Note what you changed and why. Keep the original clips and cost for the final percentage calculation. Copy the notes template in the final section to organize your evidence.
items.title: Recording Data
items.alt: Record settings, outputs, value, and the reason for each change. Core diameter is a setting; wire length is an output.

items.text: A student changes current and records clips lifted. Which variable belongs on each axis? Put current (A), the changed numerical variable, on the horizontal axis and clips lifted on the vertical axis. Plot the measured values or means and label units. If comparing iron, air, and another core material, use named categories, such as a bar graph, instead of treating materials as numerical values.
items.title: Which axes fit your question?
items.alt: A numerical-current graph places current in amperes on the horizontal axis and clips lifted on the vertical axis. Core materials instead require named categories.

items.text: Two tested current levels show a larger mean clip count at the higher current. Does that prove that doubling current always doubles lifting performance? No. State the increase for this tested setup. More current levels and evidence about the model would be needed to justify a wider rule. Clip count is a performance measure, not a direct measurement of magnetic field.
items.title: Does the evidence establish a universal rule?
items.alt: Evidence from the tested setup supports a limited comparison, but does not establish an exact rule for all currents.

items.text: A physical test gives 9, 10, and 11 clips under the same conditions. Keep all three valid observations and report their mean and spread. Do not remove 9 just to make the result look better. If a documented procedural fault makes a measurement invalid, explain the exclusion and repeat the measurement.
items.title: Should you discard a result that differs?
items.alt: Three physical measurements of 9, 10, and 11 clips should all be retained if valid.

items.text: For a physical current investigation, test more current levels and repeat each setting to check variation. For the deterministic simulation, test additional distinct designs or a controlled comparison that answers your question. Repeating identical simulation settings does not reveal random measurement uncertainty. Choose a next test that addresses your actual limitation.
items.title: What additional evidence would help?
items.alt: A physical investigation benefits from more current levels and repeats; a deterministic simulation benefits from new designs and evaluation of model limits.

items.text: Claim:  “C gave the best value among my three tested designs.”   Numerical evidence:  “A, B, and C gave 3.23, 3.50, and 3.85 clips per cost unit. Using the original fractions, C improved value by 19.1% over A.”   Reasoning:  “B lifted 42 clips, two more than C, but its greater cost reduced its value. C gave more lifting performance per cost unit.”   Limits and next step:  “This comparison identifies the best design I tested, not a universal optimum. Several settings differ, so I cannot attribute the improvement to one cause. I would next vary one setting from C, check both calculations, and continue searching.”  Notice how each sentence has a job. Use the structure with your own checked data; do not copy these invented values.

Numerical evidence: “A, B, and C gave 3.23, 3.50, and 3.85 clips per cost unit. Using the original fractions, C improved value by 19.1% over A.”

Reasoning: “B lifted 42 clips, two more than C, but its greater cost reduced its value. C gave more lifting performance per cost unit.”

Limits and next step: “This comparison identifies the best design I tested, not a universal optimum. Several settings differ, so I cannot attribute the improvement to one cause. I would next vary one setting from C, check both calculations, and continue searching.”
